newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Mass grave opened up in Liberia massacre town.
newsitem.headline: Mass grave opened up in Liberia massacre town.

text.p: Health workers have dug up 21 bodies from a mass grave in a Liberian town where scores of people were massacred by rebels last week, officials said on Friday.

Chief pathologist Dr Isaac Moses told reporters in the capital Monrovia that most of the decomposing bodies exhumed on Thursday were of women or children, shot at close range, stabbed or battered to death with blunt objects.
Residents said up to 70 bodies were buried in shallow graves around the town of Senje in Liberia's violent western Cape Mount county where the massacres occurred, he said.
Workers would search for other mass graves on the outskirts of Senje, which is 100 km (60 miles) west of Monrovia.
"Among the 21 exhumed were the bodies of nine male adults and the rest females, including infants," he added.
Aid workers and U.N. officials reported that about 25 civilians were confirmed massacred in Senje on September 28 and that many more bodies were believed to be in nearby bushes.
The killings are blamed on guerrillas of the ULIMO-J militia of ethnic Krahn warlord General Roosevelt Johnson.
Health workers ventured into Senje after the ECOMOG African peacekeeping force in Liberia sent troops backed by tanks on Wednesday to dismantle ULIMO-J roadblocks on highways.
Guerrillas disrupted efforts by international relief agencies to feed thousands of starving villagers trapped by renewed militia clashes in the region.
Western Liberia, notably around the Krahn stronghold town of Tubmanburg, remains the most volatile part of the country, which has been tormented by civil war since December 1989.
Battles there, notably between ULIMO-J and the Nigerian-led ECOMOG, were followed by all-out militia warfare in Monrovia in April that shattered an accord on ending the civil war.

ULIMO-J and a rival militia, the Madingo-dominated ULIMO-K, have clashed there in recent weeks in a new threat to yet another peace accord signed by Liberia's squabbling warlords in Nigeria in August.

The local church charity, Concerned Christian Community, which works in the Tubmanburg area, estimates that about 2,000 people have been died of starvation or in factional clashes between the rival ULIMOs since July.
Moses said another government health team was expected in Tubmanburg on Friday to try to dig up bodies of victims of starvation believed to be buried around the provincial capital.
Moses supervised the exhuming and reburial of hundreds of bodies from mass graves around Monrovia after the capital exploded into ethnic warfare last April.
The World Health Organisation's resident representative in Liberia, Dr Joseph Kamara, said it was necessary to exhume the bodies from mass graves for proper burial for health reasons.
Despite symbolic gestures and promises of disarmament, Liberia's warring factions have yet to start demobilising their 60,000 guerrillas in earnest.

The new disarmament timetable agreed in Nigeria provides for elections in May after ECOMOG would have disarmed guerrillas. But the force, sent to Liberia in 1990 by the 16-member Economic Community of West African States, says it is waiting for troop reinforcements from regional states.
More than 150,000 people have died in the conflict in Liberia, which was founded by freed American slaves in 1847 as Africa's first independent republic.
